sermons.life_context: In 1834 Finney was pastor of the Second Free Presbyterian Church at Chatham Street Chapel, New York. By his own account he had fallen ill with cholera during his installation there in 1832. In 1834 he also sailed to the Mediterranean for his health, spending weeks at Malta and Sicily, and he recalled being away about six months.

Finney gave these lectures as pastor of the Second Free Presbyterian Church at Chatham Street Chapel, after about six months away on a Mediterranean voyage for his health. His Memoirs say he spent the voyage home in anguished prayer, fearing that revivals would decline across the country. In 1835 he accepted Oberlin's theology professorship while keeping his New York pulpit.

sermons.life_context: Finney was then pastor of the Second Free Presbyterian Church, which met at Chatham Street Chapel in New York, and had held that post since September 1832. His Memoirs say that when he returned from a health voyage to Malta and Sicily in 1834, he found mob excitement over slavery in the city. In 1835 he accepted Oberlin's theology professorship and kept his New York pulpit.

sermons.life_context: The volume does not say when this sermon was first preached. In 1836, the year the collection appeared, Finney became pastor of New York's Broadway Tabernacle (from 10 April). He also left the Presbytery that year and from then on identified as a Congregationalist. He had held Oberlin's professorship of theology since 1835.

Finney was then an itinerant revivalist, ordained in 1824 and married to Lydia Andrews since October that year. In January 1826 he had begun his Oneida County revivals at Rome, followed by work in Utica through 1826 and early 1827. Later, in July 1827, Nathan Beman and Lyman Beecher convened a ministers' conference at New Lebanon to debate his 'new measures'; it ended without agreement.

No date or place of delivery is recorded for this sermon. It was published in 1836, the year Finney moved from the Chatham Street Chapel pastorate to the Broadway Tabernacle (April 1836). That year he also left the Presbytery, and from then on he identified as a Congregationalist. He had also been Oberlin's professor of theology since 1835.

In 1837 Finney was pastor of New York's Broadway Tabernacle until he resigned on 6 April. He had also held Oberlin's professorship of theology since 1835. His daughter Julia was born in March 1837, and that same year he settled at Oberlin as pastor of its First Congregational Church.

This lecture was given in New York in 1837, the year Finney's New York ministry ended. He had been pastor of the Broadway Tabernacle since April 1836, the year he left the Presbytery and began to identify as a Congregationalist. He resigned the Tabernacle on 6 April 1837. He had held Oberlin's theology professorship since 1835 and settled at Oberlin in 1837.

No delivery date is recorded for this sermon. When it was printed in January 1849, Finney was pastor of Oberlin's First Congregational Church and professor of theology there. His first wife, Lydia, had died in December 1847. In November 1848 he married Elizabeth Ford Atkinson, a widow.

Finney was then in London, more than a year into a British preaching tour. He and his second wife, Elizabeth, had arrived at Southampton in November 1849, and the tour began at Houghton, Huntingdonshire. He was still pastor of Oberlin's First Congregational Church, and the tour lasted until early 1851.

When this sermon was printed in November 1851, Finney had recently returned from his 1849–51 British preaching tour. On 26 August he had been elected president of Oberlin College. He took on the presidency while keeping his pastorate of the First Congregational Church and his theology teaching.

When the sermon was printed in June 1853, Finney was in his second year as president of Oberlin College. He was also pastor of Oberlin's First Congregational Church and taught theology. His daughter Delia had died in 1852.

When this sermon was printed in August 1858, Finney was president of Oberlin College, pastor of Oberlin's First Congregational Church and professor of theology. His second preaching tour of Britain came soon after. Christian History dates its start to December 1858, while Oberlin's archives date the visit 1859–60.

When the Oberlin Evangelist printed this sermon in July 1860, Finney was on his second British preaching tour. Christian History dates that tour from December 1858 to August 1860, and in 1860 the paper reported him preaching at Bolton and Manchester. The sermon speaks to 'this Institution' and its students, so it was evidently preached earlier, on a date that is not recorded.
